A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PermLLM research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material relocated or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning, utility, and access-control experiments with Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-0.1-7B on four datasets, including appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds PubMedQA results and experiments evaluating a prompt-based access-control baseline.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same Activate, SVD-based Merge, and Union mechanisms, including domain-to-adapter mapping and inference procedures. The added prompt-based method is a comparison baseline, not a revision to PermLLM.

E1.justification: v2 adds biomedical context/question/answer data from PubMedQA, partitioned into ten security domains using embedding clustering. This substantially extends coverage to artificially constructed domains within a common medical corpus, where utility gaps behave differently from the original four benchmarks. All original datasets remain.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates full fine-tuning and ordinary LoRA as utility baselines but lacks an evaluated prompt-based access-control comparator. New Appendix E adds a domain-prefix baseline across both models and all five datasets, with loss, DDI, and UGI comparisons. This introduces a substantive alternative enforcement approach; it is not a demonstrated reproduction of the cited prompt-based systems.

E3.justification: The added PubMedQA evaluation uses 200,000 training and 11,269 test records, with GTE embeddings and k-means defining ten domains. The new baseline receives domain prefixes during training and inference and is also evaluated with two to five active SimpleQA domains. Existing dataset splits, model sizes, training budgets, and evaluation metrics are retained.

E4.justification: New Figure 11 tests the prompt baseline's sensitivity to increasing active-domain counts on SimpleQA. Added baseline loss curves in Figures 4–8 examine training and generalization despite its weak access-control results. The original Activate/Merge/Union scaling analyses remain, including v1 Figure 8 as v2 Figure 9.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across domains or domain pairs and explicitly acknowledge only one fine-tuning run per parameter setting. New result entries follow the existing reporting practice; no additional seeds, repeated-run estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: Original benchmark table values are retained, but substantial new results are added. PubMedQA has two-domain UGI values of approximately 0.00–0.01 in Table 3, while the single-domain Ref attack reaches DDI AUC-ROC 1.00 for both models in Table 2. New Table 9 reports prompt-baseline AUC-ROC values of 0.50–0.59, accompanied by near-zero UGI in Figures 10–11. These are additional settings and comparisons, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: Section 2.3, audit-game step 5, adds absolute-value bars around the relevance-difference expression before comparing it with the access-advantage threshold. This changes the stated acceptance condition when the difference can be negative. The principal definitions, assumptions, RAG formalism, and Appendix B proofs otherwise remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the access-control formalism, three PermLLM mechanisms, and DDI/UGI auditing metrics. The abstract and introduction expand the reported evaluation from four datasets to five, but this adds supporting evidence without redefining those core claims.

C2.justification: v2 attributes PubMedQA's near-zero UGI to similar underlying domain distributions and adds the limitation that DDI is only as good as the best available membership-inference attack. Appendix E explains the prompt baseline's failure through small prefix differences and acknowledges that other prompt structures might perform better. Existing scalability and authentication limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds PubMedQA's record format, GTE/k-means construction, maximum token length, and license. Appendix E documents applying domain prefixes during both fine-tuning and inference. Existing optimizer, LoRA, hardware, and training details are retained; these additions document the new experiments rather than establish changes to the old implementation.

R1.justification: v2 adds the PubMedQA dataset paper and connects already cited prompt-based access-control work to the new baseline discussion. The broader positioning relative to AdapterSwap, RAG, privacy, and indistinguishability remains substantially unchanged; most reference changes are renumbering or bibliographic formatting.

P1.justification: The main narrative and existing technical sections remain largely intact. Local wording edits clarify the description of absolute access control and shorten discussion passages; acknowledgements are expanded. A new prompt-baseline Appendix E is inserted, moving the existing MIA appendix to F without substantially rewriting it.

P2.justification: Experimental displays are substantially expanded: Figure 2 and Tables 1–8 gain PubMedQA groups, and Figures 4–7 change from three to four panels with relocated legends to include the prompt baseline. New Figure 8, Figures 10–11, and Table 9 display additional experiments. The old Figure 8 is retained as Figure 9.

improvement.justification: v2 provides useful empirical checks absent from v1: a prompt-based comparison and a PubMedQA case exposing UGI's limited sensitivity while distinguishing stronger from weaker DDI attacks. The new attack-dependence caveat also improves qualification of the evidence. These are meaningful but bounded gains: only a simple prompt-prefix baseline is tested, and single-run evaluation and the core methodological limitations remain.
